name: Ultherapy / HIFU skin tightening

lead: Ultherapy uses focused ultrasound to heat deep skin layers so that skin looks lifted over the following months. It was first FDA cleared in 2009 for brow lifting, later for the neck, chin and chest.
Studies are mostly small device trials; reported improvement is gradual and typically lasts one to two years.

paras: Focused ultrasound creates tiny heat zones in the dermis and SMAS layer with imaging guidance, said to prompt new collagen and elastin over time.
Common effects are redness, swelling, pain and tingling. Rarer reports include bruising, numbness, temporary facial weakness, burns and fat atrophy. It is done by trained clinicians.

lead: Ultherapy is a non-invasive cosmetic procedure that uses micro-focused ultrasound with visualization (MFU-V) to heat deep skin layers, with the aim of lifting and tightening skin on areas such as the brow, neck and under the chin. It is made by Ulthera, Inc., which Merz Aesthetics acquired in 2014.[1] Other devices using high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) for skin tightening are sold under different names.

The device received its first FDA clearance in 2009 for non-invasive eyebrow lifting, with later clearances for the neck and under-chin area in 2012 and for lines and wrinkles on the decolletage in 2014.[1]

Evidence for skin tightening comes mainly from small device trials. One summary of pooled data reports investigator-rated improvement of about 92 percent at 90 days, while patient-reported satisfaction ranged from roughly 42 to 59 percent.[1] Note that source itself relies partly on clinic and manufacturer material.
infobox: Ulthera, Inc.; owned by Merz Aesthetics since 2014[1]
Appear over about 2 to 6 months; typically last 1 to 2 years per the source[1]

paras: Focused ultrasound creates small zones of thermal coagulation in the dermis and in the deeper SMAS layer while sparing the surface epidermis. The resulting heat injury is said to trigger a healing response that produces new collagen and elastin, and ultrasound imaging lets the clinician place the energy at chosen depths.[1] General reviews of HIFU describe it as a technique for non-invasive tissue heating, used far more widely in tumour ablation than in cosmetics.[2][3]

Ulthera was founded in 2004 as a spin-off from Guided Therapy Systems and grew from HIFU research in the late 1990s and early 2000s. The company reports one million treatments by 2017 and more than three million by 2025, and launched the PRIME platform in 2024.[1]
Reported results appear gradually over months. Evidence for body areas such as the abdomen and arms is described as mostly pilot data.[1]

Common effects are redness, swelling, tenderness, pain and tingling or numbness. Less common effects include bruising, prolonged numbness and temporary facial weakness. Burns and fat atrophy have been reported mostly in post-marketing surveillance, and one small study reported a 23 percent complication rate.[1] Open wounds and implants in the treatment area are listed as contraindications.[1]

Registered small device studies include trials in neck lifting (n=18), the ageing hand (n=7), acne scars (n=20), upper inner arm laxity (n=15), a brow-lift and face-and-neck study of the Octave system (n=50), decolletage wrinkles (n=99), surgical scars, spider veins and gene expression after treatment.[4][5][6][7][8][9][10] The registry listings reviewed do not themselves report outcomes.
